account: On the evening of Saturday 15 February 2020, during Storm Dennis, a 400-year-old oak fell across the A31 at Sturminster Marshall, Dorset. It hit two Tesla Model X cars going in opposite directions. Laurence Sanderson of Brentwood, Essex, was driving his wife Anna and three children to a half-term holiday. The other car was a Tesla loan vehicle driven by Josh Whitelock of Wimborne, with Kitty McConnell and her mother Julia. It also stopped suddenly. Anna Sanderson had two black eyes and bruising. Nobody was seriously hurt. That night Laurence Sanderson wrote to Tesla and Elon Musk on Twitter: "Autopilot kicked in and saved us." On 17 February 2020 he told the Mirror that the car was on Autopilot, that the emergency braking kicked in and that the trunk landed on the hood. On the same day Fred Lambert, the editor in chief of Electrek, questioned the drivers' account. He argued that Tesla's emergency braking could not detect a tree that fell from beside the road. He suggested that the drivers may have braked themselves, and he called for the vehicle logs. On 19 February 2020 Whitelock told the Bournemouth Echo that he was not sure whether the car's automatic brakes were enabled. He credited the car's other safety features. The same day the Mirror reported that Elon Musk had replied: "Glad you're all ok." On 25 February 2020 Anna Sanderson repeated the family's account on BBC London. No source reports that the logs were released.

ai_role.statement: Laurence Sanderson told the Mirror that the emergency braking stopped his car. Josh Whitelock said that he was not sure whether his loan car's automatic brakes were enabled. Electrek's editor Fred Lambert argued on 17 February 2020 that the braking system could not recognize a tree falling into the road, and he suggested that the drivers may have braked themselves without knowing it. He called for the vehicle logs. No source reports vehicle logs, a Tesla statement, a police finding or an engineering assessment.

fields.account: On the evening of Saturday 15 February 2020, during Storm Dennis, a 400-year-old oak fell across the A31 at Sturminster Marshall, Dorset. It hit two Tesla Model X cars going in opposite directions. Laurence Sanderson of Brentwood, Essex, was driving his wife Anna and three children to a half-term holiday. The other car was a Tesla loan vehicle driven by Josh Whitelock of Wimborne, with Kitty McConnell and her mother Julia. It also stopped suddenly. Anna Sanderson had two black eyes and bruising. Nobody was seriously hurt. That night Laurence Sanderson wrote to Tesla and Elon Musk on Twitter: "Autopilot kicked in and saved us." On 17 February 2020 he told the Mirror that the car was on Autopilot, that the emergency braking kicked in and that the trunk landed on the hood. On the same day Fred Lambert, the editor in chief of Electrek, questioned the drivers' account. He argued that Tesla's emergency braking could not detect a tree that fell from beside the road. He suggested that the drivers may have braked themselves, and he called for the vehicle logs. On 19 February 2020 Whitelock told the Bournemouth Echo that he was not sure whether the car's automatic brakes were enabled. He credited the car's other safety features. The same day the Mirror reported that Elon Musk had replied: "Glad you're all ok." On 25 February 2020 Anna Sanderson repeated the family's account on BBC London. No source reports that the logs were released.

produced_by: Automatic Emergency Braking active on a Tesla Model X whose cameras and radar register an obstacle entering its path

purpose: Tesla's Autopilot hardware and software provide driver assistance and active safety features including Automatic Emergency Braking. It detects obstacles the car may hit and applies the brakes. Stopping short of a falling tree is that intended use as the drivers describe it.

ratings.reason: A 400-year-old oak struck two cars at the hood. Eight people walked away with, at worst, two black eyes, a bump on the head and bruising. Laurence Sanderson and the Mirror call the braking life-saving. That claim rests on his account, and no telemetry or official assessment is reported. The second driver was unsure whether the brakes were enabled.
